course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 3
firstTopic.summary: How the Seven Years' War, British imperial reform, colonial self-government, and Enlightenment ideas set the stage for independence and the first experiments in republican government, 1754–1800.

writingQuizzes.title: LEQ: How much did the Revolution change society?

topic.title: Taxation Without Representation
topic.summary: How Parliament's efforts to raise revenue and assert authority after 1763 united the colonists in protest, what arguments they used, and how resistance moved from boycotts to war.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: The Stamp Act of 1765 was a British law that
choices: taxed imported sugar and molasses and strengthened enforcement against smuggling in colonial ports
closed the port of Boston and limited self-government in Massachusetts after the destruction of tea there
taxed printed materials such as newspapers and was the first direct tax Parliament placed on colonists
allowed the East India Company to sell tea in the colonies at a lower price than colonial merchants
questions.explanation: The Stamp Act placed a direct tax on printed materials, which led to organized protest throughout the colonies.
choiceExplanations: This describes the Sugar Act of 1764.
This describes the Coercive Acts of 1774.
The Stamp Act placed a direct tax on printed materials, which led to organized protest throughout the colonies.
This describes the Tea Act of 1773.
questions.distinguisher: The Sugar Act choice is close because it was the previous revenue measure, but it taxed imports and not printed materials.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Parliament passed the Declaratory Act in 1766 at the same time that it repealed the Stamp Act. The Declaratory Act
choices: promised that the colonies would never again be taxed by Parliament without the approval of their assemblies
claimed that Parliament had the power to make laws for the colonies in all cases whatsoever
declared the colonies independent of Parliament in matters of trade and left taxes to the colonial assemblies
ended the Navigation Acts so that colonial merchants could trade freely with France and Spain
questions.explanation: By repealing the tax but asserting its authority, Parliament made clear that it would not give up its claim to govern the colonies.
choiceExplanations: The act asserted Parliament's authority and made no such promise.
By repealing the tax but asserting its authority, Parliament made clear that it would not give up its claim to govern the colonies.
The act asserted Parliament's authority over the colonies.
The Declaratory Act did not end the Navigation Acts.
questions.distinguisher: The promise choice is close because repeal looked like a concession, but Parliament insisted on its power.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766?
choices: Colonial protests, including boycotts, hurt British merchants and showed widespread resistance
French and Spanish officials threatened to attack British colonies unless the tax was ended
The act had raised so much money that Parliament no longer needed to collect the tax
The Stamp Act Congress voted to leave the empire, and Parliament repealed the act to win it back
questions.explanation: Boycotts and protests cost British merchants business and showed that the tax could not be enforced.
choiceExplanations: Boycotts and protests cost British merchants business and showed that the tax could not be enforced.
Foreign powers did not force the repeal.
The tax was difficult to collect and raised little money because of the protests.
The Stamp Act Congress petitioned Parliament and did not vote to leave the empire.
questions.distinguisher: The raised-money choice reverses the situation, because the tax was widely resisted and hard to collect.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The colonial slogan “no taxation without representation” expressed the belief that
choices: colonists should refuse to pay any taxes to any government unless the money was spent in their own town
colonists should elect members of Parliament who would then represent them in London
only property owners should pay taxes because they had the most interest in the colonial government
colonists should be taxed only by representatives they had chosen, such as those in their own assemblies
questions.explanation: Colonists argued that as British subjects they could be taxed only with the consent of their representatives, and they pointed to their assemblies.
choiceExplanations: Colonists accepted taxes by their own assemblies and did not reject all government.
Most colonists did not ask for seats in Parliament.
The slogan concerned who had the right to tax, not who should pay.
Colonists argued that as British subjects they could be taxed only with the consent of their representatives, and they pointed to their assemblies.
questions.distinguisher: The Parliament-seats choice is close because the slogan mentions representation, but most colonists wanted their own assemblies to tax them.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a difference between the British and colonial views on representation in the 1760s?
choices: Britain argued that colonial assemblies alone should tax the colonies, while colonists argued for taxes by Parliament
Britain argued that representation required a vote for every adult, while colonists argued for property requirements
Britain argued that Parliament represented all British subjects, while colonists said only their assemblies could tax them
Britain argued that representation was unnecessary in the empire, while colonists argued for a king chosen by the colonies
questions.explanation: British officials relied on the idea of virtual representation, and many colonists rejected it, pointing to their own assemblies.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the two positions.
Neither side based its argument on universal adult suffrage.
British officials relied on the idea of virtual representation, and many colonists rejected it, pointing to their own assemblies.
British officials claimed that Parliament did represent the colonists, and colonists did not seek a colonial king.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed-positions choice is close because both sides used the word representation, but it swaps who held each view.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: The Coercive Acts of 1774 were passed in response to which of the following?
choices: The Boston Massacre, in which British soldiers killed five colonists in a crowd in 1770
The destruction of tea in Boston Harbor by colonists protesting the Tea Act
The refusal of colonial merchants to pay duties under the Townshend Acts in the years after 1767
The meeting of the First Continental Congress, which called for a boycott of British goods
questions.explanation: Parliament punished Massachusetts by closing the port of Boston and limiting its self-government, and the colonies called these measures the Intolerable Acts.
choiceExplanations: The massacre occurred four years earlier, and the Coercive Acts were a response to the Tea Party.
Parliament punished Massachusetts by closing the port of Boston and limiting its self-government, and the colonies called these measures the Intolerable Acts.
The Townshend duties were mostly repealed in 1770.
The Congress met after the Coercive Acts.
questions.distinguisher: The Boston Massacre choice is close because it was also a Boston crisis, but the Coercive Acts followed the Tea Party.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes how women contributed to the colonial resistance to British policies?
choices: Women formed groups that spun cloth at home and gave up British tea in support of boycotts
Women served in the House of Burgesses and voted on the boycott resolutions that colonial assemblies passed
Women wrote the petitions sent to Parliament and signed them as official representatives of the colonies
Women commanded militia units in towns near Boston and led the Sons of Liberty in port cities
questions.explanation: Women supported the boycotts by making cloth at home and giving up imported goods, and they ran farms and shops.
choiceExplanations: Women supported the boycotts by making cloth at home and giving up imported goods, and they ran farms and shops.
Women could not hold seats in colonial assemblies.
Colonial assemblies and congresses sent official petitions.
Women did not command militia units or lead the Sons of Liberty.
questions.distinguisher: The petition choice is close because women took part in the cause, but they did not sign official petitions as representatives.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains how many colonists responded to economic shortages and the British military occupation of some regions?
choices: Most colonists left the cities for the frontier and refused to take part in the conflict
Colonial leaders ended the boycotts and asked Parliament to station more soldiers in the port cities
Men and women mobilized in large numbers to give financial and material support to the Patriot cause
Wealthy merchants took over the colonial governments and sold supplies only to the British army
questions.explanation: The hardships strengthened the movement because people gave money, supplies, and labor to the Patriot cause.
choiceExplanations: Many colonists stayed and supported the movement.
Leaders continued the boycotts and resisted British troops.
The hardships strengthened the movement because people gave money, supplies, and labor to the Patriot cause.
Many merchants supported the Patriot cause.
questions.distinguisher: The frontier choice is close because some colonists did move west, but the movement drew broad support.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the historical situation in which the excerpt was written?
choices: Colonial merchants were responding to the Sugar Act and preparing to petition Parliament for its repeal
British officials were announcing new regulations for the western lands after the Seven Years' War
Delegates to the Constitutional Convention were debating how to divide power between the states and the national government
Colonial representatives were explaining their break with Britain after years of disputes over taxes and authority
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Second Continental Congress in 1776, when war with Britain was already under way.
choiceExplanations: The Sugar Act was passed in 1764, and the excerpt is from the Declaration of Independence of 1776.
The excerpt is a complaint against British rule, not an announcement from British officials.
The Constitutional Convention met in 1787, after the Declaration was adopted.
The Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Second Continental Congress in 1776, when war with Britain was already under way.
questions.distinguisher: The Sugar Act choice is close because it also concerned colonial grievances, but the excerpt was written twelve years later, when the colonies were declaring independence.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.3, KC-3.1.II.A and KC-3.1.II.B: colonial leaders based resistance on the rights of British subjects and objected to taxes imposed without colonial consent
stimulusBlocks.attribution: The Declaration of Independence, adopted by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, from the list of complaints against King George III
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Declaration of Independence (1776), list of grievances. Project Gutenberg eBook #16780.
stimulusBlocks.note: “Others” refers to Parliament, whose authority over the colonies the Declaration rejects. “Pretended” means “claimed.”
stimulusBlocks.text: He has combined with others to subject us to a jurisdiction foreign to our constitution, and unacknowledged by our laws; giving his Assent to their Acts of pretended legislation: For quartering large bodies of armed troops among us: For protecting them, by a mock Trial, from Punishment for any Murders which they should commit on the Inhabitants of these States: For cutting off our Trade with all parts of the world: For imposing taxes on us without our Consent: For depriving us, in many cases, of the benefits of Trial by Jury:

questions.subskillText: Identify a source’s point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main claim of the excerpt?
choices: The colonists could no longer trade with Britain until Parliament repealed the Navigation Acts
The Crown and Parliament had violated the colonists' rights through taxes, troops, and the denial of jury trials
The colonial assemblies should have the same powers as Parliament throughout the British Empire
The colonists wished to remain loyal to Parliament while objecting only to the presence of the army
questions.explanation: The excerpt accuses the king and Parliament of imposing a foreign jurisdiction, taxing without consent, quartering troops, and denying jury trial.
choiceExplanations: The excerpt lists grievances, including cutting off trade, but it does not demand the repeal of the Navigation Acts.
The excerpt accuses the king and Parliament of imposing a foreign jurisdiction, taxing without consent, quartering troops, and denying jury trial.
The excerpt does not call for equal powers for the assemblies.
The excerpt accuses the king and Parliament of many acts, not only of stationing an army.
questions.distinguisher: The army choice is close because quartering troops is one of the grievances, but the excerpt lists several others.

questions.prompt: The grievances listed in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: British efforts after 1763 to raise revenue and tighten control, such as the Stamp Act and Coercive Acts
The Great Awakening, which led colonists to question religious authority and traditional church membership
The Articles of Confederation, which gave Congress the power to quarter troops in the states in wartime
The Proclamation of 1763, which allowed colonists to settle west of the Appalachian Mountains
questions.explanation: The grievances in the excerpt summarize colonial complaints about taxes, troops, trade restrictions, and legal changes after 1763.
choiceExplanations: The grievances in the excerpt summarize colonial complaints about taxes, troops, trade restrictions, and legal changes after 1763.
The Great Awakening was a religious movement, and it did not produce these grievances.
The Articles came after the Declaration, and the grievances concern British actions.
The Proclamation restricted settlement, and it does not explain the grievances in the excerpt.
questions.distinguisher: The Proclamation choice is close because it was also a source of friction, but it restricted settlement and is not the context for these grievances.
